text: We're moving to a second cloud warehouse platform now, and it comes from a genuinely different lineage than Snowflake. Databricks SQL runs on top of Apache Spark, and its syntax traces back through Spark SQL to Hive SQL. In practice that heritage lands close to standard SQL for most everyday statements — but it carries its own real conventions you should expect to adjust to, not assume will match what you already know.

First, identifier quoting: Databricks SQL uses backticks, not T-SQL's square brackets and not ANSI double quotes. Select bracket Order Date bracket from bracket Sales Orders bracket in T-SQL becomes select backtick Order Date backtick from backtick Sales Orders backtick in Databricks SQL. And here's a nice shortcut: if you've already covered MySQL earlier in this course, this is the exact identical convention — nothing new to learn, just recognize it.

Second, a concept worth knowing by name even if you don't need to master its internals for this course: Delta Lake. Databricks SQL tables are usually backed by Delta Lake, an open table format that adds transactional guarantees and version history on top of files sitting in cloud storage. Create table orders, with columns, using DELTA. When Databricks documentation or an error message mentions Delta Lake, it's talking about the storage layer underneath the tables your SQL queries against — not some separate add-on product you need to opt into separately.

Third, and this is the one genuinely new syntax pattern in this lesson: LATERAL VIEW explode, for working with array and map columns. Picture a table where one column holds an array of item names per order. LATERAL VIEW explode of item underscore names, as item underscore name, turns each element of that array into its own output row, still paired with its parent order id. Conceptually, this is doing exactly what CROSS APPLY does in T-SQL — expanding a correlated value per source row — but the syntax bears no resemblance at all. It's a Spark-specific keyword combination, not a JOIN-family keyword.

So here's the shape of Databricks SQL to carry forward: backticks for identifiers, same as MySQL; Delta Lake as the storage layer underneath most tables you'll query; and LATERAL VIEW explode as the array-expansion pattern, conceptually like CROSS APPLY but syntactically its own thing entirely.

Next lesson, we'll move quickly through two more cloud warehouses — BigQuery and Redshift — covering just enough orientation to recognize their SQL when you see it, since this course stays focused on language, not administration. See you there.
